summary:
Cantabria has no statute of its own on legal gender recognition or on anti-discrimination protection; the region stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, which applies uniformly to all autonomous communities. A visitor to Cantabria therefore deals with the same administrative route as anywhere in Spain: adults may rectify the sex entry on their civil registry record without prior surgical reassignment, and the right is grounded in the free development of personality under Article 10.1 of the Spanish Constitution.

The same statute defines and sanctions discriminatory conduct and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, sexual identity, gender expression and sexual characteristics, voids discriminatory contract clauses, and obliges public bodies to collect discrimination data broken down by the protected cause. It also mandates measures adapted to rural circumstances, a provision with direct bearing in a region where much of the population lives outside Santander.

The sources assembled for this record contain no Cantabria-specific ordinance, enforcement series, court decision or incident finding. Exposure in the region is consequently shaped by how the national framework operates locally rather than by any separate regional rule, and the national assessment carries the weight of the entry.
tangentialFactors:
Protection across Spain is not uniform, and the contrast is drawn with the region of Madrid, whose government repealed its non-discrimination law and its local conversion-therapy ban insofar as it covers trans people in 2023. Cantabria has taken no comparable step, and nothing in the sources indicates any regional rollback here.

Official framing of Spain as a destination is favourable: UK foreign travel advice describes the country as generally tolerant and progressive for LGBT+ travellers, and a travel operator guide rates it safe and welcoming while noting that attitudes outside the large cities can be more conservative. That caveat bears on Cantabria directly, since the region's smaller towns and rural interior are precisely where the national law's rural-adaptation mandate is meant to bite.
localsOnly:
Residents of Cantabria use the same Civil Registry route as the rest of Spain: a request before the registry office, with no diagnosis of gender dysphoria and no requirement of two years of medical treatment. Recognition is available from age 12 under the conditions set by the statute, which also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Regional and municipal administrations in Cantabria are bound by the statute's data-collection obligation and by its mandate to adapt anti-discrimination measures to rural circumstances, so residents pursuing a complaint or a service adjustment deal with regional bodies operating under national rules rather than under a Cantabrian ordinance of their own.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Cantabria-specific enforcement record was located: the inventory contains no regional court decision applying the discrimination aggravating circumstance, no regional hate-crime or discrimination statistics, and no documented incident involving a trans resident or visitor. Whether the regional administration has issued its own rural-adaptation measures under Ley 4/2023 is unresolved on these sources.

The July 2026 Vigo decision and the January 2026 Valencia juvenile case, both cited in the national layer, fall outside this region and are carried by the parent record; their presence there does not establish any enforcement pattern in Cantabria.
